messages.text: I'm working on garnet-type LLZO solid electrolytes with lithium metal anodes. We keep seeing short circuits at current densities well below what the bulk properties predict. Post-mortem SEM suggests lithium filaments running along grain boundaries rather than through grains. My working hypothesis is that grain boundaries have lower ionic conductivity and higher electronic conductivity, so lithium gets reduced inside them. Does that match what's known?

Your hypothesis is consistent with a substantial line of thinking in the field. Grain boundaries in garnet electrolytes can have different chemistry, including lithium deficiency, segregated dopants or secondary phases, which may increase local electronic conductivity. That would allow lithium to nucleate inside the electrolyte rather than only at the interface. Others emphasise mechanical factors, such as stress concentration at boundaries, voids and cracks that lithium can wedge open. It's likely a combination, and the dominant mechanism may depend on processing and microstructure.

That fits with what we see. Our samples sintered at higher temperature have bigger grains and seem to last longer, but they also have more lithium loss, so it's confounded. I want to separate electronic leakage from mechanical cracking. I was thinking of measuring electronic conductivity with blocking electrodes on samples with different grain sizes. Is that a reasonable first step?

Yes, DC polarisation with lithium-blocking electrodes is a sensible way to quantify electronic conductivity, and comparing grain sizes will help. To decouple grain boundary effects, you could also do impedance spectroscopy to separate bulk and grain boundary contributions, and control lithium loss by using mother powder during sintering. Correlating electronic conductivity and grain boundary density with critical current density would test your hypothesis directly.

chats.title: Watching dendrites form in real time

messages.text: All our dendrite evidence comes from post-mortem cross sections, which is frustrating because we only see the end state and sample prep might create artefacts. I'd really like to watch lithium penetrate the electrolyte while the cell is cycling. I've heard of synchrotron X-ray tomography for this, but I've never used a beamline and don't know how to get access. What are the options?

Operando imaging options include synchrotron X-ray tomography, which can resolve lithium filaments and cracks in 3D over time; lab-based X-ray CT, which has lower resolution and slower acquisition; operando optical microscopy using a side-view cell geometry; and in-situ electron microscopy for very small cells. Synchrotron access usually goes through competitive proposals at user facilities, and success often depends on having an experienced beamline user or staff scientist involved who knows cell design and data reconstruction.

That's what I was afraid of. Our group has no synchrotron experience and I don't think we'd write a competitive proposal on our own. We are good at making the electrolyte pellets and cycling them, so I'd love to partner with someone who already does operando tomography of batteries. They'd bring the imaging expertise, we'd bring well characterised samples.

That kind of partnership is common and works well. Imaging groups often look for interesting, well-characterised samples, and your ability to make controlled microstructures, for instance different grain sizes, is valuable to them. You'd also need to co-design an operando cell that fits the beamline, maintains stack pressure and allows X-ray transmission through a thin electrolyte. Preparing a short summary of your samples, failure behaviour and key questions would make it easier to approach potential collaborators.

I'm trying to standardise how we measure critical current density in our Li/LLZO/Li symmetric cells. Right now we step up current every few cycles until shorting, but results vary a lot between nominally identical pellets. I think part of it is interfacial contact and part is random defects at grain boundaries. How do people get reproducible CCD numbers?

CCD is notoriously sensitive to protocol. Key factors include the current step size and dwell time, areal capacity per step, temperature, stack pressure, and interface preparation. Reproducibility improves if you remove surface carbonates before assembly, control lithium thickness, and report full voltage profiles rather than only the shorting current. Running more cells per condition and reporting distributions, rather than single values, helps account for defect-driven variability.

Reporting distributions makes sense. I suspect the spread is real and tells us something, maybe the weakest grain boundary path determines failure. If that's true, CCD would follow something like weakest-link statistics. I could test that by varying pellet thickness and area and seeing if failure probability scales the way it should.

That's a nice idea. If failure is controlled by the most vulnerable defect or grain boundary path, then larger electrode areas should fail at lower current on average, and you could fit the distribution to a Weibull model. Thickness dependence would tell you whether penetration needs a full connected path or whether nucleation is the limiting step. That would be a neat way to link microstructure statistics to failure.

There's a lot of talk about applying high stack pressure to solid-state cells to keep the lithium in contact with the electrolyte. We see better cycling at higher pressure too. But I wonder whether pressure fixes the interface or just pushes lithium creep into voids and masks the problem, which would come back in a real pack where you can't apply that much pressure. Is there evidence either way?

Both interpretations have support. Pressure promotes lithium creep, which fills voids formed during stripping and keeps the interface contact area high, lowering local current density and delaying dendrite initiation. But very high pressure can also drive lithium into cracks or pores in the electrolyte, which can actually accelerate shorting. Many lab results use pressures far above what's practical in commercial packs, so the improvements may not translate.

So it's double-edged. I'm curious whether there's a pressure window where contact is maintained without forcing lithium into grain boundaries. We have a small press rig and could run cells at several pressures. I'm not sure what range is meaningful though.

A scan from low single-digit MPa up to around 10 to 20 MPa would cover the practically relevant and typical lab regimes. Track interfacial resistance, void formation after stripping, and time to short for each. If you see an optimum, it would be worth checking post-mortem whether higher pressures show more lithium intrusion at grain boundaries. Use at least three cells per pressure so you can tell a real trend from cell-to-cell scatter, and keep temperature constant, since lithium creep is strongly temperature dependent.

We got some interesting input on our grain boundary hypothesis. Dr. Elena Varga at Northfield Institute shared unpublished atom probe data showing aluminium and lanthanum segregation at grain boundaries in samples similar to ours. That would support the idea that boundaries have different local chemistry and maybe higher electronic conductivity. How should I think about connecting segregation to dendrite growth in my cycling experiments?

Segregation data is a useful link. If dopants or secondary phases at boundaries lower the band gap or introduce electronic states, lithium ions could be reduced within the boundary before reaching the anode. To connect this to your cycling, you could vary the dopant level or sintering conditions to change segregation, then measure electronic conductivity and critical current density. If failure correlates with segregation strength, that supports a chemical mechanism rather than purely mechanical cracking.

We actually have three batches with different aluminium doping levels. I could cycle cells from each batch and do cross sections afterwards to see whether the lithium paths follow boundaries more in the high aluminium samples. I'd need to be careful though, since doping also changes grain size.

That's a good experiment, and you're right about the confound. You could try to match grain size across batches by adjusting sintering time, or measure grain size and include it as a covariate. Quantifying the fraction of lithium paths that are intergranular versus transgranular in each batch would give you a clear metric to compare. Measuring electronic conductivity on each batch with blocking electrodes would close the loop between composition, transport and failure.

While we wait to figure out synchrotron access, I'm wondering whether we could do some operando optical microscopy ourselves. A side-view cell where we look at the edge of the LLZO pellet while cycling. I'm not sure the resolution would be enough to see dendrites starting at grain boundaries, and I have no experience building these cells.

Optical microscopy can capture lithium growth at the edge of a cell at micron resolution, which is sometimes enough to see filaments emerging and propagating, though not the earliest nucleation inside grain boundaries. The main challenges are sealing the cell to keep it inert, applying stack pressure while keeping the edge visible, and making sure the edge behaves like the bulk. Polishing the edge can introduce surface defects that become preferential paths.

Right, so the edge might be a special case. I think optical is useful as a stopgap but what we really need is 3D imaging inside the pellet while it's cycling. I'd rather find a group that has already built operando cells for tomography or electron microscopy than spend a year reinventing it badly.

That seems like a sensible prioritisation. Groups with established operando cells have already solved sealing, pressure and alignment problems, and they know the imaging artefacts. You could still use a simple optical cell for quick screening of conditions, then bring the most interesting samples to a collaborator for 3D operando imaging. Having screening data ready also makes beamtime more efficient, because you can arrive knowing which conditions produce the most informative failures.

Many papers add thin interlayers like gold or aluminium oxide between lithium and LLZO to improve wetting. They do lower interfacial resistance in our hands, but I'm not convinced they help with grain boundary penetration, since dendrites seem to nucleate inside the electrolyte too. Am I right that interlayers only address the interface part of the problem?

Largely yes. Interlayers mostly improve wetting and current distribution at the interface, reducing hot spots that initiate dendrites from the anode side. They don't change the electronic properties or mechanics of grain boundaries deep in the electrolyte, so they won't stop lithium nucleating internally if that's a main mechanism. That said, by homogenising current, they can delay failure even if the internal mechanism remains.

That's my thinking too. I want to design an experiment that separates interface-initiated dendrites from internally nucleated ones. Maybe cells with and without interlayers, cycled to just before shorting, then sectioned to see where lithium deposits are located. If internal deposits are present regardless of interlayer, that's telling.

That design is good. Sectioning at several stages before shorting would reveal the sequence of events. Pair it with careful sample prep, such as cryo or ion milling under inert conditions, to avoid smearing lithium. Quantifying isolated lithium deposits inside the electrolyte, not connected to either electrode, would be strong evidence for internal nucleation. Mapping how the number of such deposits changes with cycling stage would also tell you whether internal growth precedes or follows interface penetration.

I ran the stack pressure scan. Interfacial resistance drops steadily up to about 8 MPa, and cells last longer. Above that, at 15 MPa, two of four cells shorted early. Post-mortem shows lithium in some cracks. So it seems like there's a sweet spot, but I'm still not sure if the improved cycling at moderate pressure is real interface improvement or just masking void formation. How could I tell?

One way is to measure void formation directly. You could cycle at different pressures and then image the interface for voids, or use impedance during stripping to track contact loss in real time. If moderate pressure maintains contact without lithium intrusion, then it's improving the interface. If voids still form but are refilled by creep, that's masking, and you'd expect failure once pressure is reduced or cycling rate increases.

Reducing the pressure mid test is a good idea. If cells cycled at 8 MPa suddenly degrade when dropped to 2 MPa, that would mean the pressure was compensating rather than fixing anything. I think that's the more honest test of whether the interface is good.

Exactly, a pressure step down test reveals whether the interface is intrinsically stable. You could also compare with cells that have an interlayer at the same pressures; if interlayer cells tolerate pressure reduction better, that indicates a genuine interface improvement rather than mechanical compensation. Tracking impedance continuously through the step down would show how quickly contact is lost, which is useful for estimating how a real pack would behave.

I collected shorting times for about 40 cells across two grain sizes. The distributions look broad, and plotting them on Weibull axes they're roughly linear, with the fine-grained samples having a lower characteristic current and similar shape parameter. Does that support the weakest-link grain boundary idea, or am I over-reading a straight line?

A linear Weibull plot with consistent shape and a shift in scale is compatible with weakest-link failure, where finer grains provide more boundary paths and thus more potential weak links. But Weibull fits can look linear for many distributions with 20 points per group. To strengthen the case, test whether the scale parameter changes with electrode area as predicted, and compare against alternative distributions like lognormal.

Good point about the area scaling, that's the real prediction. I'll make cells with two electrode areas from the same batch. If larger area fails at lower current by the predicted amount, that would be strong evidence that failure is controlled by the density of vulnerable boundaries.

That's a clean test. Keep everything else constant: same batch, same thickness, same pressure, same interface preparation. If you see the area dependence, you could even estimate the density of critical defects per unit area, which would be a nice quantitative link between microstructure and dendrite failure. Aim for a similar number of cells per area so the comparison has comparable statistical power, and record any cells excluded for assembly problems.

I'm drafting a short note to approach groups who do operando X-ray tomography or operando electron microscopy on batteries. What we offer: controlled LLZO microstructures with different grain sizes and doping, statistics on failure, and post-mortem cross sections. What we need: the ability to actually see lithium enter grain boundaries during cycling. How should I frame it so it's appealing to them?

Lead with the scientific question, whether lithium nucleates inside grain boundaries or propagates from the interface, and why operando imaging is uniquely able to answer it. Then highlight what you bring: well-characterised samples with systematically varied microstructure, a statistical dataset of failure behaviour, and complementary post-mortem analysis. Suggest a concrete first experiment, such as imaging two grain sizes under identical conditions, and note practical matters like cell compatibility and sample dimensions.

I like starting with the question. I'll also say that we can make samples thin enough for transmission and that we're happy to adapt our pellet geometry to their cell. I really don't want to try to learn tomography reconstruction from scratch, so the collaboration has to be genuinely two-sided.

That's the right attitude, and offering to adapt sample geometry signals that you've thought about their constraints. Clarify roles and shared outputs early, such as co-authorship and data sharing. A two-sided collaboration where you supply samples and failure statistics and they provide imaging expertise is attractive because each side contributes something the other can't easily do. Attaching one or two representative post-mortem images and a failure statistics plot to the note would make it concrete and memorable.
